blocks.text: Ten minutes after an uncomplicated vaginal birth, the midwife notices blood pooling on the floor beneath the bed. The mother, a fifth-time mother who laboured quickly, is pale and her pulse has risen from 84 to 118. On the abdomen the uterine fundus is soft and sits above the umbilicus. In the next ten minutes the team has to find out why she is bleeding and stop it, because a woman can lose a litre of blood in a few minutes.

blocks.markdown: **Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH)** is blood loss of 500 mL or more from the genital tract within 24 hours of birth. **Primary PPH** occurs within 24 hours; **secondary PPH** occurs between 24 hours and 12 weeks. UK guidance grades primary PPH as **minor** (500 to 1000 mL), **moderate** (1000 to 2000 mL) and **severe** (above 2000 mL). It is a leading cause of maternal death worldwide. Women tolerate the loss because the circulating volume has expanded in pregnancy, but compensation can mask a severe loss until sudden collapse.

blocks.title: The four Ts
blocks.text: The causes of primary PPH are remembered as the four Ts. Tone: failure of the uterus to contract (atony), accounting for about 70 percent. Tissue: retained placenta, membranes or clots. Trauma: genital tract lacerations, uterine rupture, uterine inversion or surgical bleeding. Thrombin: coagulopathy, either pre-existing (for example inherited bleeding disorders, anticoagulants) or acquired (for example disseminated intravascular coagulation after abruption or sepsis).

blocks.markdown: The physiological mechanism explains the commonest cause. After the placenta separates, bleeding from the placental bed is stopped by contraction and retraction of the myometrium, which compresses the spiral arteries (the 'living ligatures'). If the uterus is **overdistended** (twins, polyhydramnios, macrosomia), **exhausted** (prolonged or very rapid labour, high parity), **prevented from contracting** (retained tissue, a full bladder, placenta praevia) or **chemically relaxed** (some anaesthetics, chorioamnionitis), tone is lost and bleeding continues. Clinically, **tone** gives a soft, boggy uterus above the umbilicus; **tissue** gives an incomplete placenta; **trauma** gives bleeding despite a well-contracted firm uterus; **thrombin** gives blood that fails to clot and bleeding from multiple sites.

rows: Overdistension, prolonged labour, high parity, uterotonic exposure
Rub up a contraction, empty the bladder, give uterotonics
Retained placenta, retained cotyledon, membranes, clot
Incomplete placenta on inspection, uterus poorly contracted
Remove clots, examine placenta, manual removal in theatre if needed
Perineal or cervical tear, uterine rupture, inversion
Bleeding despite firm uterus; bright red continuous bleeding
Examine and repair in good light with analgesia; surgery for rupture or inversion
Failure of blood to clot; oozing from cannula sites
Send clotting and fibrinogen; replace with blood products
blocks.caption: The four Ts.

blocks.title: Measuring blood loss by weighing
blocks.prompt: After a vaginal birth, soaked swabs and pads weigh 1650 g in total. Their dry weight was 400 g. A drape collection bag holds 600 mL of measured blood. Assuming 1 g of blood has a volume of 1 mL, what is the estimated blood loss and its grade?

steps.text: Subtract the dry weight to obtain the weight of blood in the swabs.
Add the measured volume in the drape.
Classify: 1850 mL lies between 1000 and 2000 mL, which is a moderate (major) PPH, and a major obstetric haemorrhage response is needed.

blocks.answer: Estimated blood loss is 1850 mL, a moderate (major) PPH.

blocks.markdown: **Stepwise management** begins with **calling for help** and starting resuscitation in parallel: oxygen, two large-bore cannulae, bloods (full blood count, crossmatch, coagulation with fibrinogen), warmed fluids and early blood products, and monitoring. **Medical**: rub up a contraction (uterine massage), empty the bladder, give **oxytocin for treatment** (5 units by slow intravenous injection, or 10 units intramuscularly if there is no intravenous access) followed by an **oxytocin infusion** (40 units in 500 mL over 4 hours); note that 10 units intramuscularly is the *prophylaxis* dose at birth, whereas the treatment dose is 5 units slow IV; give **ergometrine** (teaching example: 500 micrograms intramuscularly) unless there is hypertension or pre-eclampsia, because it causes vasoconstriction; give **carboprost** (teaching example: 250 micrograms intramuscularly, repeated at 15-minute intervals up to a maximum of 8 doses) unless the woman has asthma, because it can cause bronchospasm; and **misoprostol** (teaching example: 800 micrograms sublingually) as an alternative. Give **tranexamic acid** (teaching example: 1 g intravenous over 10 minutes) as soon as PPH is recognised and within 3 hours of birth. **Mechanical**: **bimanual uterine compression**, and **intrauterine balloon tamponade** when medical therapy fails. **Surgical**: compression sutures (for example B-Lynch), uterine or internal iliac artery ligation, interventional radiological embolisation, and **hysterectomy** as a life-saving last resort. Always examine for and repair trauma and ensure the placenta is complete. Doses here are for teaching: check against current RCOG, NICE and local guidance before use.

items: Call for help and resuscitate (ABC, two cannulae, bloods, warmed fluids).
Identify the cause using the four Ts; rub up a contraction and empty the bladder.

Uterotonics: oxytocin 5 units slow IV (or 10 units IM if no IV access) then an infusion of 40 units in 500 mL over 4 hours, then ergometrine or carboprost if not contraindicated, then misoprostol; tranexamic acid.
Mechanical: bimanual compression and intrauterine balloon tamponade.
Theatre: examine under anaesthesia, remove tissue, repair trauma.
Surgical: compression sutures, arterial ligation, embolisation, hysterectomy.

blocks.title: Calculating an oxytocin infusion dose
blocks.prompt: Following a 5 unit slow IV treatment dose of oxytocin, an infusion of 40 units in 500 mL is run through a pump at 125 mL per hour. How many units per hour is delivered and what is the total dose in 4 hours? (Teaching example only: check against current RCOG, NICE and local guidance.)

steps.text: Find the concentration in units per mL.

blocks.answer: 10 units per hour, delivering all 40 units over 4 hours.

blocks.markdown: **Risk factors and prevention.** Antenatal risk factors include previous PPH, multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, macrosomia, placenta praevia or abruption, high parity, obesity, maternal age, anaemia and bleeding disorders. Intrapartum factors include induction and augmentation of labour, prolonged labour, instrumental delivery, caesarean section and retained placenta. Prevention rests on **identifying risk** and planning delivery in an appropriate unit, **correcting anaemia** before labour, **active management of the third stage** (prophylactic oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly after birth of the baby, which is the prophylaxis dose and differs from the treatment dose of 5 units slow IV; check against current RCOG, NICE and local guidance, with controlled cord traction after signs of separation) and prompt treatment of bleeding. Women at high risk may have an intravenous cannula sited in labour, and tranexamic acid may be offered.

blocks.title: Do not wait for the blood loss to reach a number
blocks.text: Visual estimation of blood loss underestimates the true amount, especially in large losses. Act on the clinical picture (tachycardia, pallor, a soft uterus) rather than a visible volume, and measure loss by weighing swabs and collecting drapes.

blocks.title: Tone is the commonest cause but never the only one
blocks.text: Always check the placenta and examine the genital tract. A firm uterus with continuing bleeding means trauma until proven otherwise, and non-clotting blood means a coagulopathy that uterotonics will not fix.

points: PPH is blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours of birth (primary); causes are tone, tissue, trauma and thrombin, with tone responsible for most cases.
Management is stepwise: help and resuscitation, uterine massage, uterotonics and tranexamic acid, mechanical tamponade, then surgery.
Ergometrine is avoided in hypertension and pre-eclampsia, and carboprost is avoided in asthma.
Risk is reduced by identifying risk factors, correcting anaemia and active management of the third stage.

questions.stem: A woman delivers twins at 36 weeks and then bleeds heavily. On examination the uterus is soft and boggy and the fundus is above the umbilicus. The placenta is complete and there are no lacerations. What is the most likely cause?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: an overdistended uterus from twins fails to contract, giving a soft boggy uterus.
distractorRationale.c: There are no lacerations and trauma gives a firm uterus.

questions.explanation: A boggy uterus after multiple pregnancy indicates uterine atony, the commonest cause of PPH. The complete placenta and lack of lacerations exclude tissue and trauma.

questions.stem: After a forceps delivery, a woman bleeds continuously with bright red blood. The uterus is firm and contracted at the level of the umbilicus and the placenta was complete. Which cause is most likely?

distractorRationale.c: Correct: continuous bright bleeding with a firm uterus after instrumental birth indicates a cervical or vaginal laceration.
distractorRationale.d: Coagulopathy gives non-clotting blood and generalised oozing.

questions.explanation: A firm contracted uterus excludes tone, and a complete placenta excludes tissue. Instrumental delivery is a recognised risk factor for cervical and vaginal tears, so the genital tract must be examined and repaired.

questions.stem: A woman with pre-eclampsia (blood pressure 158/104 mmHg) has a PPH due to uterine atony after oxytocin has been given. Which second-line uterotonic should be avoided?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ergometrine is a vasoconstrictor that can precipitate severe hypertension.
distractorRationale.b: Carboprost is avoided in asthma, not hypertension.
distractorRationale.d: An oxytocin infusion is safe, though hyponatraemia is possible with large fluid volumes.

questions.explanation: Ergometrine causes vasoconstriction and a rise in blood pressure, so it is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia. Carboprost, misoprostol and oxytocin are alternatives.

questions.stem: A woman has had oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost and tranexamic acid for atony, and bleeding persists with a soft uterus and ongoing blood loss of 2200 mL. She is being resuscitated. Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the same drugs and observe for another hour
Proceed to theatre for examination under anaesthesia and intrauterine balloon tamponade, with surgical options prepared
Perform hysterectomy without trying any other measure

questions.correctOptionText: Proceed to theatre for examination under anaesthesia and intrauterine balloon tamponade, with surgical options prepared

distractorRationale.a: Delaying escalation risks irreversible shock and coagulopathy.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: when uterotonics fail, mechanical tamponade and surgery follow.
distractorRationale.d: Hysterectomy is a last resort after less invasive measures.

questions.explanation: After medical therapy fails, escalate to mechanical and then surgical options while continuing resuscitation. Balloon tamponade and examination under anaesthesia treat atony and also exclude retained tissue or trauma.

questions.stem: Which intervention at the time of birth most effectively reduces the risk of postpartum haemorrhage?

options.text: Active management of the third stage with prophylactic oxytocin after birth of the baby
Allowing the placenta to deliver after more than 2 hours
Early cord clamping to reduce the third stage

questions.correctOptionText: Active management of the third stage with prophylactic oxytocin after birth of the baby

distractorRationale.a: Correct: oxytocin promotes uterine contraction and reduces PPH.
distractorRationale.b: Prolonged third stage raises haemorrhage risk.
distractorRationale.c: Cord clamping timing does not prevent PPH.

questions.explanation: Prophylactic oxytocin given with the birth of the baby causes sustained uterine contraction and reduces blood loss. It is the cornerstone of active management of the third stage.

questions.stem: True or false: Prolonged oxytocin augmentation of labour is a risk factor for uterine atony and PPH.
questions.explanation: Prolonged exposure of oxytocin receptors to oxytocin causes receptor desensitisation, and long labours exhaust the myometrium, so tone is more likely to fail after delivery. Women who have had augmentation are therefore counted as higher risk for PPH.

questions.stem: After a caesarean section, suction canister volume is 700 mL (including 150 mL of amniotic fluid), and soaked swabs weigh 1100 g with a dry weight of 300 g. Assume 1 g of blood equals 1 mL. Calculate the estimated blood loss in mL.
questions.explanation: Blood in the canister is 700 minus 150, which is 550 mL, and the swabs hold 1100 minus 300, which is 800 mL. The total is 550 plus 800, which is 1350 mL.

questions.stem: Oxytocin 40 units in 500 mL is infused at 250 mL per hour (teaching example only). How many units per hour is the woman receiving?
questions.explanation: The concentration is 40 divided by 500, which is 0.08 units per mL. At 250 mL per hour this delivers 20 units per hour. The standard treatment infusion is 40 units in 500 mL over 4 hours (125 mL per hour); check against current RCOG, NICE and local guidance.

questions.stem: A woman has a 1.5 litre PPH after a vaginal birth with a soft uterus. Describe the stepwise management, covering resuscitation, medical, mechanical and surgical measures.
markingGuide: Call for help and activate major obstetric haemorrhage protocol
Resuscitation: oxygen, two large-bore cannulae, bloods including crossmatch and coagulation, warmed fluids and blood products
Uterine massage and emptying the bladder

Uterotonics: oxytocin 5 units slow IV (or 10 units IM if no IV access) followed by an infusion of 40 units in 500 mL over 4 hours, then ergometrine (unless hypertension), carboprost (unless asthma) or misoprostol
Tranexamic acid within 3 hours of birth
Check the placenta and examine the genital tract to exclude tissue and trauma
Mechanical: bimanual compression and intrauterine balloon tamponade
Surgical: compression suture, uterine or internal iliac artery ligation, embolisation, hysterectomy as last resort
questions.explanation: Management escalates from least to most invasive while resuscitation continues in parallel. The cause must be identified and treated at each step.

questions.stem: Explain the four causes of primary PPH, giving one clinical clue and one risk factor for each, and discuss how the risk of PPH can be reduced.
markingGuide: Tone: uterine atony; soft boggy uterus; risk factors overdistension, prolonged labour, high parity
Tissue: retained placenta or membranes; incomplete placenta; risk factors previous retained placenta, placenta accreta
Trauma: lacerations, rupture or inversion; bleeding with a firm uterus; instrumental delivery, macrosomia
Thrombin: coagulopathy or DIC; blood fails to clot; abruption, anticoagulants, bleeding disorders
Prevention: risk assessment and delivery in appropriate setting
Active management of the third stage with prophylactic oxytocin (10 units IM, the prophylaxis dose) and controlled cord traction
Prompt recognition, and tranexamic acid when bleeding starts
questions.explanation: Each T has a different mechanism and treatment, so identifying the cause directs therapy. Prevention depends on recognising risk factors early and using prophylactic uterotonics.
